Tempo markings and BPM: what Allegro, Andante, and Moderato mean

The speed of a piece is written at the top of the first page, either as an Italian word such as Allegro, as a metronome mark such as ♩ = 120, or both. This page lists the common words with their usual BPM and explains how to turn any marking into a number you can set on a metronome or in a player.

BPM and metronome marks

BPM (beats per minute) is the number of beats in one minute. ♩ = 60 means sixty quarter notes per minute, one per second; ♩ = 120 is twice as fast. Older editions write M.M. ♩ = 60, after Maelzel's metronome, and ♩ = c. 60 (circa) means "about 60".

From the BPM you can work out how long the music lasts: one beat is 60 ÷ BPM seconds, and a 4/4 measure is four beats.

Tempo markings chart

The words describe a character as much as a speed, so the numbers are only a guide. The ranges below are the ones most references give; metronome scales and other books differ by a few BPM; the same word is also taken faster or slower depending on the period, the composer, and the piece. "This app" is the tempo the app uses when it finds only the word on the page.

Scroll the table sideways →

MarkingUsual BPMThis appMeaning
Grave25–4540very slow, solemn
Largo40–6050slow and broad
Lento45–6055slow
Larghetto60–6663rather slow (a little faster than largo)
Adagio66–7670slow, at ease
Adagietto72–7675a little faster than adagio
Andante76–10880at a walking pace
Andantino80–10888a little faster than andante (usually)
Moderato108–120108at a moderate speed
Allegretto112–120112moderately fast
Allegro120–156132fast, lively
Vivace156–176160lively and fast
Vivacissimo172–176172very lively
Presto168–200180very fast
Prestissimo200+200as fast as possible

From slowest to fastest. When a word is combined with another (Allegro moderato), the speed is between the two.

When the beat is not a quarter note

A metronome mark counts whatever note is shown before the equals sign. In 6/8 the beat is usually a dotted quarter, and in 2/2 (cut time) it is a half note. To compare tempos, or to set a player that counts quarter notes, multiply by the length of the beat in quarter notes.

Scroll the table sideways →

On the pageMultiplyEnter in the appBeat unit
♪ = 120× 0.5♩ = 60eighth note
♩. = 60× 1.5♩ = 90dotted quarter (6/8, 9/8, 12/8)
half note = 60× 2♩ = 120half note (2/2, cut time)
dotted half = 50× 3♩ = 150dotted half (fast 3/4, one beat per measure)

A dotted note is 1.5 times the plain note: a dotted quarter is 1.5 quarter notes.

Words that modify or change the tempo

WordMeaning
molto, assaivery (Allegro molto: very fast)
poco, un pocoa little
ma non troppobut not too much (Allegro ma non troppo)
con motowith motion, a little faster (Andante con moto)
più mosso / meno mossofaster / slower than before, from here on
ritardando (rit., ritard.), rallentando (rall.)gradually slower
accelerando (accel.)gradually faster
a tempo, Tempo I (primo)back to the tempo before the change / the first tempo
rubatofreely, stretching and pressing the time
fermatahold this note or rest longer than written

How this app sets the tempo

When you open a photo or PDF, the app looks at the top part of the first page for a metronome mark (the number after =) and uses it. If there is none, it looks for one of the words in the chart and uses the value in the "This app" column. If it finds neither, it plays at ♩ = 120. You can change the tempo at any time with −5 / +5, by typing a number, or with the slider (20–300).

  • The number is always used as quarter notes per minute. For ♩. = 60 or a half-note beat, enter the converted value from the table above.
  • The whole piece is played at one tempo. Changes later in the piece (rit., a new tempo, fermatas) are not followed; change the tempo by hand while it plays if you need to.
  • A MusicXML file opens at the tempo written in it.

The tempo is read with text recognition, so a marking in an unusual font, or a photo that is blurred or dark, may be missed. See how to photograph sheet music and the guide.
